Question 1 (Least squares and matrix calculations)

Set the random seed to 43201. Generate n=100n=100 observations with p=5p=5 predictors according to

xij∼iidN(0,1),εi∼iidN(0,0.72), x_{ij}\overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}N(0,1), \qquad \varepsilon_i\overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}N(0,0.7^2),

with all predictors and errors generated independently. Let

𝐗=[𝟏𝐱1⋯𝐱5],𝛃=(3,1.4,−0.9,0.7,0,1.1)𝖳, \mathbf X = \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf 1 & \mathbf x_1 & \cdots & \mathbf x_5 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad \boldsymbol\beta = (3,1.4,-0.9,0.7,0,1.1)^{\mathsf T},

and generate

𝐲=𝐗𝛃+𝛆. \mathbf y=\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta+\boldsymbol\varepsilon.

  1. Generate the data and report the dimensions and rank of 𝐗\mathbf X. Calculate the least-squares estimate 𝛃̂\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta} using a numerically stable least-squares routine, without explicitly calculating (𝐗𝖳𝐗)−1(\mathbf X^{\mathsf T}\mathbf X)^{-1}. Compare the estimates with the coefficients used to generate the data.

  2. Calculate the fitted values, the residual vector 𝐫=𝐲−𝐗𝛃̂\mathbf r=\mathbf y-\mathbf X\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}, and the training root mean squared error

RMSE⁡=(1n∑i=1nri2)1/2. \operatorname{RMSE} = \left( \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}r_i^2 \right)^{1/2}.

  1. Report ‖𝐗𝖳𝐫‖∞\lVert\mathbf X^{\mathsf T}\mathbf r\rVert_\infty. Explain why this value should be close to zero and what it tells us about the residual vector.

Solution

a. The matrix 𝐗\mathbf X has 100 rows because there are 100 observations. It has 6 columns: one intercept column and five predictor columns. Its rank is 6, which means none of its columns can be made from a combination of the other columns.

The estimated coefficients are

(3.0063,1.4172,−0.8883,0.7953,0.0484,1.1319)𝖳. (3.0063, 1.4172, -0.8883, 0.7953, 0.0484, 1.1319)^{\mathsf T}.

These estimates are close to the true values used to create the data. They are not exactly the same because random error was added to the response.

b. A fitted value is the response predicted by the model, so 𝐲̂=𝐗𝛃̂\widehat{\mathbf y}=\mathbf X\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}. A residual is the difference between an observed response and its fitted value, so 𝐫=𝐲−𝐲̂\mathbf r=\mathbf y-\widehat{\mathbf y}. The training RMSE is approximately 0.67640.6764. This means that the model’s fitted values are about 0.67640.6764 units away from the observed responses on average.

c. The value of ‖𝐗𝖳𝐫‖∞\lVert\mathbf X^{\mathsf T}\mathbf r\rVert_\infty is approximately 8.9×10−148.9\times10^{-14}. This number is so small that it is effectively zero; the small nonzero value is caused by computer rounding. Least squares chooses the coefficients so that the residual vector is perpendicular to every column of 𝐗\mathbf X. Therefore, multiplying 𝐗𝖳\mathbf X^{\mathsf T} by the residuals should give values close to zero. Because 𝐗\mathbf X includes an intercept column, this also means the residuals add up to approximately zero.

set.seed(43201)

n <- 100
p <- 5

x <- matrix(rnorm(n * p), nrow = n, ncol = p)
epsilon <- rnorm(n, mean = 0, sd = 0.7)

X <- cbind(
  Intercept = 1,
  x1 = x[, 1],
  x2 = x[, 2],
  x3 = x[, 3],
  x4 = x[, 4],
  x5 = x[, 5]
)

beta <- c(3, 1.4, -0.9, 0.7, 0, 1.1)
y <- drop(X %*% beta + epsilon)

# (a) Dimensions, rank, and stable least squares
rank_X <- qr(X)$rank

# QR-based calculation; does not explicitly form inverse(t(X) %*% X)
beta_hat <- qr.solve(X, y)

coefficient_comparison <- data.frame(
  term = colnames(X),
  true = beta,
  estimate = beta_hat,
  difference = beta_hat - beta
)

print(dim(X))
[1] 100   6
print(rank_X)
[1] 6
print(coefficient_comparison)
               term true   estimate difference
Intercept Intercept  3.0  3.0063210 0.00632099
x1               x1  1.4  1.4171604 0.01716042
x2               x2 -0.9 -0.8883453 0.01165468
x3               x3  0.7  0.7952834 0.09528339
x4               x4  0.0  0.0484378 0.04843780
x5               x5  1.1  1.1319341 0.03193413
# (b) Fitted values, residual vector, and training RMSE
fitted_values <- drop(X %*% beta_hat)
residuals <- y - fitted_values
rmse <- sqrt(mean(residuals^2))

# The full vectors are stored in fitted_values and residuals
print(head(data.frame(fitted = fitted_values, residual = residuals)))

print(normal_equation_error)

Question 2 (Gaussian likelihood for linear regression)

Continue with the data from Question 1. Suppose

𝐘∣𝐗∼Nn(𝐗𝛃,σ2𝐈n). \mathbf Y\mid\mathbf X \sim N_n\left(\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta,\sigma^2\mathbf I_n\right).

The log-likelihood, including the constant term, is

ℓ(𝛃,σ2)=−n2log⁡(2πσ2)−12σ2(𝐲−𝐗𝛃)𝖳(𝐲−𝐗𝛃). \ell(\boldsymbol\beta,\sigma^2) = -\frac{n}{2}\log(2\pi\sigma^2) -\frac{1}{2\sigma^2} (\mathbf y-\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta)^{\mathsf T} (\mathbf y-\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta).

  1. For fixed σ2\sigma^2, explain why maximizing ℓ(𝛃,σ2)\ell(\boldsymbol\beta,\sigma^2) over 𝛃\boldsymbol\beta is equivalent to minimizing the residual sum of squares. What does this imply about the maximum-likelihood estimate of 𝛃\boldsymbol\beta?

  2. For fixed 𝛃\boldsymbol\beta, differentiate the log-likelihood with respect to σ2\sigma^2 and derive its maximum-likelihood estimate. Calculate this estimate at 𝛃̂\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta} and compare it with the unbiased estimate of σ2\sigma^2. Explain why the two denominators differ.

  3. Let

𝐞x2=(0,0,1,0,0,0)𝖳. \mathbf e_{x_2}=(0,0,1,0,0,0)^{\mathsf T}.

Using the variance estimate from part b, plot

ℓ(𝛃̂+t𝐞x2,σ̂MLE2) \ell\left( \widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}+t\mathbf e_{x_2}, \widehat{\sigma}_{\mathrm{MLE}}^2 \right)

over a grid of tt values from −1.25-1.25 to 1.251.25. State where the maximum occurs and explain why this agrees with the least-squares result.

Solution

a. When σ2\sigma^2 is fixed, the only part of the log-likelihood that changes with 𝛃\boldsymbol\beta is the residual sum of squares (RSS). The RSS has a negative sign in front of it. Therefore, making the RSS smaller makes the log-likelihood larger. This means the value of 𝛃\boldsymbol\beta that maximizes the likelihood is the same least-squares estimate found in Question 1.

b. Let v=σ2v=\sigma^2 and let RSS\operatorname{RSS} denote the residual sum of squares. For fixed 𝛃\boldsymbol\beta,

∂ℓ∂v=−n2v+RSS2v2. \frac{\partial\ell}{\partial v} = -\frac{n}{2v}+\frac{\operatorname{RSS}}{2v^2}.

Setting this derivative equal to zero gives

σ̂MLE2=RSSn. \widehat{\sigma}_{\mathrm{MLE}}^2 = \frac{\operatorname{RSS}}{n}.

For these data, the RSS is 45.747645.7476, so the MLE is 0.45750.4575. The unbiased estimate is 45.7476/(100−6)=0.486745.7476/(100-6)=0.4867. The MLE divides by 100 because that value comes directly from maximizing the likelihood. The unbiased estimate divides by 94 because six coefficients were estimated from the data, using six degrees of freedom.

c. The graph reaches its highest point at t=0t=0. At t=0t=0, the coefficient vector is exactly 𝛃̂\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}. Moving tt away from zero changes the x2x_2 coefficient, increases the RSS, and lowers the log-likelihood. This agrees with Question 1 because the least-squares estimate is also the maximum-likelihood estimate of 𝛃\boldsymbol\beta.

# Write your code for all computational parts of Question 2 here.

rss <- sum(residuals^2)

# (b) Variance estimates
sigma2_mle <- rss / n
sigma2_unbiased <- rss / (n - qr(X)$rank)

print(rss)
[1] 45.74759
print(sigma2_mle)
[1] 0.4574759
print(sigma2_unbiased)
[1] 0.4866765
# (c) Log-likelihood profile in the x2 coefficient direction
log_likelihood <- function(beta_value, sigma2) {
  r <- y - drop(X %*% beta_value)

  -n / 2 * log(2 * pi * sigma2) -
    sum(r^2) / (2 * sigma2)
}

# beta ordering: intercept, x1, x2, x3, x4, x5
e_x2 <- c(0, 0, 1, 0, 0, 0)
t_grid <- seq(-1.25, 1.25, length.out = 501)

profile_loglik <- sapply(t_grid, function(t) {
  log_likelihood(beta_hat + t * e_x2, sigma2_mle)
})

t_at_maximum <- t_grid[which.max(profile_loglik)]
maximum_loglik <- max(profile_loglik)

print(t_at_maximum)
[1] 0
print(maximum_loglik)
[1] -102.7923
plot(
  t_grid,
  profile_loglik,
  type = "l",
  lwd = 2,
  col = "navy",
  xlab = "t",
  ylab = "Log-likelihood",
  main = "Log-likelihood along the x2 coefficient direction"
)

abline(v = 0, lty = 2, col = "red")
points(0, maximum_loglik, pch = 19, col = "red")

Question 3 (Starting values in nonconvex optimization)

Consider the function

f(x)=exp⁡(1.5x)−3(x+6)2−0.05x3, f(x)=\exp(1.5x)-3(x+6)^2-0.05x^3,

with derivative

f′(x)=1.5exp⁡(1.5x)−6(x+6)−0.15x2. f'(x)=1.5\exp(1.5x)-6(x+6)-0.15x^2.

  1. Plot f(x)f(x) over the interval [−40,7][-40,7]. Based on the plot, describe the important features of the objective function that may affect numerical optimization.

  2. Use BFGS to minimize f(x)f(x) twice, starting at x(0)=−15x^{(0)}=-15 and x(0)=0x^{(0)}=0. Supply f′(x)f'(x) to the optimizer. For each run, report the final value of xx, the final objective value, |f′(x)||f'(x)|, and whether the optimizer reported convergence.

  3. Explain why the two runs can converge to different answers. Which run gives the lower objective value? What additional evidence would be needed before claiming that this point is the global minimum?

Solution

a. The graph has two low points, called local minima, with a high point between them. It also rises very quickly on the right side. BFGS follows the local slope of the function, so it may move toward different low points when it starts in different places.

b. Starting at −15-15, BFGS stops at approximately x=−32.64911x=-32.64911, where f(x)=−390.38577f(x)=-390.38577 and |f′(x)|=8.7×10−8|f'(x)|=8.7\times10^{-8}. Starting at 00, it stops at approximately x=2.34997x=2.34997, where f(x)=−175.86262f(x)=-175.86262 and |f′(x)|=6.6×10−7|f'(x)|=6.6\times10^{-7}. Both absolute derivatives are very close to zero, and both runs report successful convergence.

c. The runs give different answers because each starting value leads BFGS toward a different local minimum. The run starting at −15-15 gives the lower function value because −390.38577<−175.86262-390.38577<-175.86262. However, a successful result only shows that BFGS found a nearby minimum. To claim that it is the global minimum, we would need to check that no lower point exists. For this one-dimensional function, we could find every point where f′(x)=0f'(x)=0, compare their function values, and also check what happens as xx goes toward positive and negative infinity.

objective <- function(x) {
  exp(1.5 * x) - 3 * (x + 6)^2 - 0.05 * x^3
}

gradient <- function(x) {
  1.5 * exp(1.5 * x) - 6 * (x + 6) - 0.15 * x^2
}

# (a) Plot the objective function
x_grid <- seq(-40, 7, length.out = 1200)

plot(
  x_grid,
  objective(x_grid),
  type = "l",
  lwd = 2,
  col = "navy",
  ylim = c(-450, 100),
  xlab = "x",
  ylab = "f(x)",
  main = "Nonconvex objective function"
)

# (b) Run BFGS from both starting values
starting_values <- c(-15, 0)

optimization_results <- lapply(starting_values, function(start) {
  optim(
    par = start,
    fn = objective,
    gr = gradient,
    method = "BFGS"
  )
})

optimization_summary <- do.call(
  rbind,
  Map(function(start, result) {
    data.frame(
      starting_value = start,
      final_x = result$par,
      final_objective = result$value,
      absolute_gradient = abs(gradient(result$par)),
      converged = result$convergence == 0
    )
  }, starting_values, optimization_results)
)

points(
  optimization_summary$final_x,
  optimization_summary$final_objective,
  pch = 19,
  col = c("blue", "red")
)
print(optimization_summary)
  starting_value    final_x final_objective absolute_gradient converged
1            -15 -32.649111       -390.3858      8.725087e-08      TRUE
2              0   2.349967       -175.8626      6.556057e-07      TRUE

Question 4 (Nearly collinear predictors)

Continue with 𝐗\mathbf X and 𝐲\mathbf y from Question 1. Set the random seed to 43202 and generate

ui∼iidN(0,1),i=1,…,n. u_i\overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}N(0,1), \qquad i=1,\ldots,n.

Define

𝐱6=𝐱1+10−4𝐮,𝐗+=[𝐗𝐱6], \mathbf x_6=\mathbf x_1+10^{-4}\mathbf u, \qquad \mathbf X_+ = \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf X & \mathbf x_6 \end{bmatrix},

and let

𝐲⋆=𝐲+10−3𝐮. \mathbf y^\star=\mathbf y+10^{-3}\mathbf u.

Use a numerically stable least-squares routine throughout.

  1. Fit 𝐲\mathbf y using 𝐗\mathbf X and 𝐗+\mathbf X_+. For each design matrix, report the condition number and training RMSE. For the augmented fit, also report the coefficients of 𝐱1\mathbf x_1 and 𝐱6\mathbf x_6.

  2. Fit 𝐲⋆\mathbf y^\star using 𝐗+\mathbf X_+. Report the changes in the coefficients of 𝐱1\mathbf x_1 and 𝐱6\mathbf x_6. Compare the two fitted-value vectors using their root mean squared difference and maximum absolute difference.

  3. Use the identity

𝐲⋆−𝐲=10(𝐱6−𝐱1) \mathbf y^\star-\mathbf y = 10(\mathbf x_6-\mathbf x_1)

to explain why the fitted values change very little while the two coefficients change substantially. What does this example suggest about interpreting separate effects for nearly collinear predictors?

Solution

a. The original matrix 𝐗\mathbf X has condition number 1.5251.525 and training RMSE 0.67640.6764. After adding x6x_6, the condition number becomes about 20,20920{,}209, but the RMSE changes only slightly to 0.67550.6755. The much larger condition number warns us that x1x_1 and x6x_6 contain almost the same information. In the augmented model, their estimated coefficients are 351.6766351.6766 and −350.2588-350.2588. These values are very large and have opposite signs, but their sum is about 1.41781.4178, which is close to the original coefficient of x1x_1.

b. After changing the response from 𝐲\mathbf y to 𝐲⋆\mathbf y^\star, the x1x_1 coefficient decreases by 10 and the x6x_6 coefficient increases by 10. Even though the coefficients change a lot, the fitted values barely change. Their root mean squared difference is 0.0010160.001016, and their largest absolute difference is 0.0025730.002573.

Because

𝐲⋆−𝐲=10(𝐱6−𝐱1), \mathbf y^\star-\mathbf y =10(\mathbf x_6-\mathbf x_1),

c. This identity shows that the small change in the response can be produced by decreasing the x1x_1 coefficient by 10 and increasing the x6x_6 coefficient by 10. Because x1x_1 and x6x_6 are almost identical, these two changes mostly cancel each other when the fitted values are calculated. The model can estimate their combined effect well, but it cannot clearly separate the effect of x1x_1 from the effect of x6x_6. Therefore, their individual coefficients should not be interpreted as reliable separate effects.

set.seed(43202)
u <- rnorm(n)

x6 <- x[, 1] + 1e-4 * u
X_plus <- cbind(X, x6 = x6)
y_star <- y + 1e-3 * u

# Use QR-based least-squares fits
fit_original <- lm.fit(x = X, y = y)
fit_augmented <- lm.fit(x = X_plus, y = y)
fit_perturbed <- lm.fit(x = X_plus, y = y_star)

condition_number <- function(design_matrix) {
  singular_values <- svd(design_matrix, nu = 0, nv = 0)$d
  max(singular_values) / min(singular_values)
}

fit_comparison <- data.frame(
  design = c("X", "X_plus"),
  condition_number = c(
    condition_number(X),
    condition_number(X_plus)
  ),
  training_rmse = c(
    sqrt(mean(fit_original$residuals^2)),
    sqrt(mean(fit_augmented$residuals^2))
  )
)

beta_augmented <- fit_augmented$coefficients
beta_perturbed <- fit_perturbed$coefficients

coefficient_comparison_q4 <- data.frame(
  response = c("y", "y_star"),
  beta_x1 = c(beta_augmented["x1"], beta_perturbed["x1"]),
  beta_x6 = c(beta_augmented["x6"], beta_perturbed["x6"])
)

coefficient_changes <- (
  beta_perturbed[c("x1", "x6")] -
    beta_augmented[c("x1", "x6")]
)

fitted_augmented <- drop(X_plus %*% beta_augmented)
fitted_perturbed <- drop(X_plus %*% beta_perturbed)
fitted_difference <- fitted_perturbed - fitted_augmented

fitted_value_comparison <- c(
  root_mean_squared_difference = sqrt(mean(fitted_difference^2)),
  maximum_absolute_difference = max(abs(fitted_difference))
)

print(fit_comparison)
  design condition_number training_rmse
1      X         1.524914     0.6763696
2 X_plus     20209.203501     0.6754668
print(coefficient_comparison_q4)

2   y_star 341.6766 -340.2588

Question 5 (Data preparation and summary statistics)

The file data/data-manipulation.csv is a small constructed data table containing an observation identifier, a group label, two numeric predictors, and a response. Some response values are missing. For analyses involving the response, use only observations with a recorded response. Do not replace a missing response with zero or a group mean.

  1. Read the data and report its dimensions, column types, number of duplicated identifiers, and number of missing values in each column. Create an analysis table containing only observations with a recorded response, and define

𝚏𝚎𝚊𝚝𝚞𝚛𝚎_𝚜𝚞𝚖=𝚡𝟷+𝚡𝟸. \texttt{feature\_sum}=\texttt{x1}+\texttt{x2}.

  1. For each group, report the number of observations, the mean response, and the mean of feature_sum. State clearly which observations these summaries describe.

  2. Sort the analysis table by response from largest to smallest and report the first three rows, including observation_id, group, response, and feature_sum. Add code checks verifying that the number of retained rows equals the number of nonmissing responses in the original data, that the analysis table has no missing response values, and that its identifiers are unique.

Solution

a. The original data have 24 rows and 5 columns. observation_id and group are stored as text, while x1, x2, and response are numeric. There are no repeated identifiers. Only response has missing values, with three missing responses. After removing those three rows, the analysis table has 21 rows. For each remaining row, feature_sum is the value of x1 + x2.

b. Each group has seven observations with a recorded response. Groups A, B, and C have mean responses of 5.60005.6000, 7.60297.6029, and 7.99717.9971. Their mean values of feature_sum are 3.60003.6000, 4.92864.9286, and 6.58576.5857. These results describe only the 21 observations with recorded responses, not all 24 rows in the original data.

c. The three largest responses are:

  • obs-22, group C: response 9.249.24 and feature_sum 6.66.6;
  • obs-16, group B: response 9.009.00 and feature_sum 5.25.2; and
  • obs-14, group B: response 8.668.66 and feature_sum 5.05.0.

The checks confirm that the analysis table has the expected number of rows, no missing responses, and no repeated identifiers.

data_file <- file.path("data", "data-manipulation.csv")

# This alternative is used when rendering from the repository root.
if (!file.exists(data_file)) {
  data_file <- file.path(
    "homework", "week-01", "data", "data-manipulation.csv"
  )
}

  data_file,
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE,
  check.names = FALSE
)

# (a) Inspect and prepare the data
dimensions <- dim(small_data)
column_types <- vapply(small_data, class, character(1))
duplicated_identifiers <- sum(duplicated(small_data$observation_id))
missing_by_column <- colSums(is.na(small_data))

analysis_data <- small_data[!is.na(small_data$response), ]
analysis_data$feature_sum <- analysis_data$x1 + analysis_data$x2

print(dimensions)

    data.frame(
      group = group_data$group[1],

Question 6 (Can 39 million Fitbit records represent US adults?)

Patten et al. (2026) describe Fitbit data from 59,018 participants in the All of Us Research Program. The dataset spans 14 years and contains more than 39 million daily step records. Participants contributed data through one of two routes:

  • Bring Your Own Device (BYOD): participants shared data from a Fitbit they already owned.
  • Wearables Enhancing All of Us Research (WEAR): invited participants received a Fitbit at no cost.

In the general activity cohort, the BYOD and WEAR groups contained 32,035 and 22,474 participants, respectively. The BYOD value is listed first in each comparison below:

  • 77.3% versus 55.1% reported being White;
  • 6.1% versus 15.2% reported annual household income between $10,000\$10{,}000 and $25,000\$25{,}000; and
  • median daily steps were 6,867 versus 5,797.

Suppose the target is the mean of the participant-specific average daily step counts among US adults during the study period, with each adult given equal weight. A researcher writes:

“This dataset contains more than 39 million daily Fitbit records. Therefore, the average of all recorded step counts should provide an accurate estimate of mean daily activity among US adults.”

  1. Are the 39 million daily records independent observations? What characteristics or behaviors could cause some participants to contribute more recorded days than others? Explain how averaging all recorded days would then weight participants unequally.

  2. BYOD participants reported a median of 6,867 daily steps, compared with 5,797 among WEAR participants. Does this comparison show that already owning a Fitbit causes people to walk more? Explain your answer and give at least one plausible alternative explanation based on how participants entered the two groups.

  3. A very large dataset can still produce a biased estimate of a population quantity when the people and observations entering the dataset are selected. Using this study, explain how selection of both participants and recorded days could make the observed data differ from the US adult population. Why might the naive average of all recorded daily step counts fail to estimate the stated target? You do not need to determine the direction of the bias.

Solution

a. The 39 million daily records are not independent because many records come from the same person. A person’s step counts on different days are likely related because their health, job, habits, and environment do not completely change each day. People can also contribute different numbers of days. For example, some may join earlier, wear and sync the device more often, or have fewer device problems. Others may have missing days because of illness, travel, privacy concerns, or inconsistent Fitbit use. If we average all daily records, a person with 1,000 recorded days receives much more weight than a person with 100 days. That does not give every adult equal weight.

b. The comparison does not prove that owning a Fitbit causes people to walk more. Participants were not randomly assigned to the BYOD and WEAR groups. People who already owned a Fitbit could have higher incomes, better access to technology, more interest in health, or higher activity levels before the study began. The demographic differences reported for the two groups also show that they are not directly comparable. Therefore, selection into the two groups could explain the difference in median steps.

c. The participants may not represent all US adults. A person had to join All of Us, enter through BYOD or WEAR, agree to share data, connect a Fitbit, and keep using it. People who complete all these steps may be different from other US adults in ways related to physical activity. The recorded days are also selected because days when a Fitbit is worn and synced may differ from days with missing data.

A very large dataset can reduce random error, but it cannot automatically fix selection bias. The simple average of all recorded days may fail because it gives more weight to participants with more records and because the people in the study may differ from the US adult population. A better first step would be to calculate one average for each participant and then give each participant equal weight. Population weights or other adjustments may also be needed to make the study participants more comparable to US adults.

Source

Patten, T., Preble, E. A., Master, H., et al. (2026). The All of Us Research Program’s wearables dataset. Nature Medicine, 32, 2302-2310.
